rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite generic “human” is exhaustive: people alive are terrified and ask one another, or each asks inwardly; brave and timid alike react to an extraordinary quake beyond endurance.
rows.anchor: أي وقال الناس ما لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is wrong with it?” asks what has become attached to the earth; the lām marks specification, yielding either what is happening in this quake or what its outcome will be.
rows.anchor: استفهام عن الشيء الذي ثبت للأرض ولزمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question personifies earth as an intentional agent whose purpose people cannot discern.
rows.anchor: نزلت الأرض منزلة قاصد مريد يتساءل الناس عن قصده من فعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because this construction usually requires a stated complement, the omitted estimate may be “why it quaked,” “what it has in this quake,” or “what it has in bringing out its burdens.”
rows.anchor: فلذلك وجب أن يكون هنا مقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the account of human ingratitude and miserliness, the question rebukes people for not knowing the time graves are overturned and inner contents gathered; their heedlessness is astonishing.
rows.anchor: فُرع على الإخبار بكنود الإنسان وشحه استفهام إنكاري عن عدم علم الإنسان بوقت بعثرة ما في القبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative hamza precedes the fāʾ of consequence because an interrogative must come at the beginning of speech.
rows.anchor: وهمزة الاستفهام قدمت على فاء التفريع لأن الاستفهام صدر الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “When” is an adverb attached to an elided object of “know”; omission leaves listeners free to supply any terrifying possibility.
rows.anchor: السامع في تقديره كل مذهب ممكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied knowledge is of punishment as recompense for ingratitude and miserliness, whose offenses vary in degree up to warranting eternal residence in Hell.
rows.anchor: ألا يعلم العذاب جزاء له على ما في كنوده وبخله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both objects of “know” are omitted without a lexical clue specifying them, leaving the threat and its terror to contextual inference; this is termed restrictive omission.
rows.anchor: ولا دليل في اللفظ على تعيين تقديرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians allow omission of both objects by ellipsis, which Ibn ʿĀshūr says is the correct analysis; Sībawayh prohibits it.
rows.anchor: وحذف كلا المفعولين اقتصارا جائز عند جمهور النحاة وهو التحقيق وإن كان سيبويه يمنعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A blazing fire” explains the preceding question “what is it?”; the implied subject is omitted in keeping with established Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: وهذا من حذف المسند إليه الذي اتبع في حذفه استعمال أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling fire “hot” is verbal emphasis because heat is inherent in fire, like the synonymous description “God’s kindled fire.”
rows.anchor: لأن النار لا تخلو عن الحمي فوصفها به وصف بما هو من معنى لفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most muṣḥafs and commentaries call it Sūrat al-Humazah; al-Bukhārī and some commentaries use “Woe to every backbiter,” while al-Fīrūzābādī records “al-Ḥuṭamah.”
rows.anchor: سميت هذه السورة في المصاحف ومعظم التفاسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan by consensus, has nine verses by consensus, and is ranked thirty-second in revelation, after al-Qiyāmah and before al-Mursalāt.
rows.anchor: عدت الثانية والثلاثين في عداد نزول السور نزلت بعد سورة القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the surah concerns polytheist mockers and slanderers, naming al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Jamīl ibn Maʿmar, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.
rows.anchor: روي أنها نزلت في جماعة من المشركين كانوا أقاموا أنفسهم للمز المسلمين وسبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report also names the Thaqīf leaders al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth and al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq; the named men were wealthy, prominent figures of the pre-Islamic era.
rows.anchor: من سادة ثقيف من أهل الطائف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamīl ibn Maʿmar later embraced Islam at the conquest of Mecca and witnessed Ḥunayn.
rows.anchor: وهذا أسلم يوم الفتح وشهد حنينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although tied to named men in the occasion report, the verse is general and covers them and others like them without naming anyone.
rows.anchor: وجاءت آية السورة عامة فعم حكمها المسمين ومن كان على شاكلتهم من المشركين ولم تذكر أسماءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah warns polytheists who made insulting and mocking Muslims a means of harming them, hoping to wear them down into abandoning Islam and returning to shirk.
rows.anchor: فغرض هذه السورة وعيد جماعة من المشركين جعلوا همز المسلمين ولمزهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Woe” invokes a bad state upon its target; here the curse is used as a threat of punishment, as in the cited warning to those who write scripture falsely.
rows.anchor: كلمة ( ويل له ) دعاء على المجرور اسمه باللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Every” signals a group habitually mocking and defaming Muslims, likely those mentioned in the surah’s reported occasion.
rows.anchor: تشعر بأن المهددين بهذا الوعيد جماعة وهم الذين اتخذوا همز المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faʿalah forms humazah and lumazah mark repeated action that has become a habit, like ḍuḥakah for someone who laughs much and luʿanah for one who curses much.
rows.anchor: صيغة تدل على كثرة صدور الفعل المصاغ منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī explains fuʿal as an intensive form of fāʿil; adding tāʾ marbūṭah can intensify it further, so the trait becomes entrenched, as discussed in al-Kashshāf.
rows.anchor: أن صيغة فعل بضم ففتح ترد للمبالغة في فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say ʿuyabah is equivalent to ʿiyābah; forms are attested variably with and without tāʾ, while some patterns occur only in vocative abuse.
rows.anchor: فمن الأمثلة ما سمع فيه الوصف بصيغتي فعل وفعلة

rows.speaker: المرادي
rows.claim: Al-Murādī reports an unnamed grammarian’s view that vocative forms such as “O traitor” are the only attested examples and cannot be extended by analogy.
rows.anchor: قال المرادي في « شرح التسهيل » قال

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh allows analogy in those vocative forms; al-Ḥarīrī applies it in his thirty-seventh maqāmah with “O ʿuqaq.”
rows.anchor: وعن سيبويه أنه أجاز القياس عليها في النداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humazah derives from hamz: fault-finding by eye, mouth-corner, or head gestures, in someone’s presence or after they leave; hamiz and hammāz are related forms.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يعيب أحد أحدا بالإشارة بالعين أو بالشّدق أو بالرأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humazah is an adjective whose modified noun (“person”) is omitted; the adjective then functions substantively, allowing “every” to be annexed to it.
rows.anchor: فلما حذف موصوفه صار الوصف قائما مقامه فأضيف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lumazah derives from lamz, confronting someone with faults; its pattern, like humazah, presents the vice as a settled trait.
rows.anchor: وصيغته دالة على أن ذلك الوصف ملكة لصاحبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The traits first describe polytheist conduct toward believers, but Muslims who treat fellow believers this way share in the warning; it is a harmful vice with degrees of severity and repetition.
rows.anchor: ومن عامل من المسلمين أحدا من أهل دينه بمثل ذلك كان له نصيب من هذا الوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among these forms of harm, striking a Muslim is counted among major sins; habitual cursing of the Companions and persistent harm likewise makes minor sins major.
rows.anchor: وسب الصحابة رضي الله عنهم وإدمان هذا الأذى بأن يتخذه ديدنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ascends upon” may mean coming swiftly with force and domination: the fire penetrates the hearts and burns them while the bodies’ exteriors burn.
rows.anchor: أي الإتيان السريع بقوة واستيلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it means disclosure and witnessing, as in 37:55: the fire knows the disbelief within hearts and burns each in proportion to its corrupt belief, by God’s calibration.
rows.anchor: فاطلع فرآه في سواء الجحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAṣf is the leaf of a crop and a collective plural of ʿaṣfah.
rows.anchor: ورق الزرع وهو جمع عصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When livestock eat crop leaves, they trample them, consume their edges, then leave them scattered on the ground, once lush and green.
rows.anchor: والعصف إذا دخلته البهائم فأكلته داسته بأرجلها وأكلت أطرافه وطرحته على الأرض بعد أن كان أخضر يانعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This image compares the People of the Elephant, after their bloom and strength, to fallen dead remains.
rows.anchor: وهذا تمثيل لحال أصحاب الفيل بعد تلك النضرة والقوة كيف صاروا متساقطين على الأرض هالكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is commonly called al-Māʿūn because that word occurs uniquely here; other recorded names include Araʾayta, used in some commentaries, a fifth-century Qayrawān muṣḥaf, and al-Bukhārī.
rows.anchor: في كثير من المصاحف وكتب التفسير

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah titles it Sūrat Araʾayta alladhī; al-Kawāshī gives the combined title al-Māʿūn wa-l-Dīn wa-Araʾayta.
rows.anchor: وكذلك في مصحف من مصاحف القيروان في القرن الخامس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other names are Sūrat al-Dīn in al-Itqān, Sūrat al-Takdhīb in al-Khafājī and Saʿdī glosses, and Sūrat al-Yatīm in al-Biqāʿī.
rows.anchor: وفي حاشيتي الخفاجي وسعدي تسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most hold the surah Meccan, with a Meccan report from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Qurṭubī transmits Qatādah’s view that it is Medinan, also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وهي مكية في قول الأكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and stated by Hibat Allāh al-Ḍarīr assigns the first three verses to Mecca and the rest to Medina, taking the latter verses as about hypocrites; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this more apparent.
rows.anchor: قيل نزلت ثلاث أولها بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Meccan dating, it is ranked seventeenth in revelation, after al-Takāthur and before al-Kāfirūn.
rows.anchor: وعدت السابعة عشرة في عداد نزول السور بناء على أنها مكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most verse counters count six; al-Ālūsī says this is the Iraqi Basran and Kufan count, while ʿAlī al-Nūrī al-Ṣafāqusī reports seven for Ḥimṣ and six elsewhere, contradicting al-Ālūsī.
rows.anchor: وعدت آياتها ستا عند معظم العادين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah exposes denial of resurrection through aggression and contempt toward the weak, withholding food from the poor, and neglect of prayer and almsgiving.
rows.anchor: من مقاصد التعجيب من حال من كذبوا بالبعث وتفظيع أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question expresses astonishment at deniers and the evil conduct their denial produces; denial itself is common, so the listener waits for the surprising orphan abuse revealed next.
rows.anchor: الاستفهام مستعمل في التعجيب من حال المكذبين بالجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding the demonstrative and relative clause after fāʾ heightens suspense, then lets the description strike and firmly occupy the listener’s attention.
rows.anchor: وفي إقحام اسم الإشارة واسم الموصول بعد الفاء زيادة تشويق حتى تقرع الصلة سمع السامع فتتمكن منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expected plain wording would directly coordinate the denial with pushing the orphan and failing to urge feeding the poor.
rows.anchor: وأصل ظاهر الكلام أن يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative singles out the denier for full recognition and inspection, or treats him as so obvious that he can be pointed at.
rows.anchor: لتمييزه أكمل تمييز حتى يتبصر السامع فيه وفي صفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ links the second attribute to the first and makes the combined attributes support the judgment; denial, orphan abuse, and neglect of feeding are joined as one person’s qualities.
rows.anchor: لإفادة تسبب مجموع الصفتين في الحكم المقصود من الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This makes resurrection denial ugly through its vices and opposition to moral responsibility, warning Muslims away from either trait as characteristic of those who reject recompense.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك كناية عن تحذير المسلمين من الاقتراب من إحدى هاتين الصفتين بأنهما من صفات الذين لا يؤمنون بالجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperfect verbs “denies,” “pushes,” and “urges” convey that the conduct is repeated and continuous.
rows.anchor: بصيغة المضارع لإفادة تكرر ذلك منه ودوامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in resurrection and recompense is the true restraint that roots good conduct until it becomes a natural habit, without needing commands or fear of enforcement.
rows.anchor: وهذا إيذان بأن الإيمان بالبعث والجزاء هو الوازع الحق الذي يغرس في النفس جذور الإقبال على الأعمال الصالحة حتى يصير ذلك لها خلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vision is physical/visual and takes one object; famous deniers and their notorious deeds are portrayed as if visibly seen.
rows.anchor: والرؤية بصرية يتعدى فعلها إلى مفعول واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ eases the second hamza in Araʾayta into an alif; Egyptian transmitters from Warsh likewise substitute alif, as Ibn ʿĀshūr recited in Tunisia, avoiding two consecutive hamzas.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع بتسهيل الهمزة التي بعد الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority pronounce both hamzas fully, while al-Kisāʾī drops the hamza after rāʾ in every verb of this form.
rows.anchor: وقرأه الجمهور بتحقيقهما .  وقرأه الكسائي بإسقاط الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative pronoun and its clause refer generically to anyone with these traits, as most exegetes hold.
rows.anchor: واسم الموصول وصلته مراد بهما جنس من اتصف بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the occasion as al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, others al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah or ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾidh al-Makhzūmī; attribution to one person would not restrict the general ruling.
rows.anchor: في عمرو بن عائذ المخزومي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report concerns Abū Sufyān before Islam: after he slaughtered a camel weekly, an orphan asked for its meat and he struck the child with a stick.
rows.anchor: في أبي سفيان بن حرب قبل إسلامه بسبب أنه كان ينحر كل أسبوع جزورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report names Abū Jahl, who was guardian to an orphan; when the child came unclothed asking for his own money, Abū Jahl shoved him violently.
rows.anchor: كان وصيا على يتيم فأتاه عريانا يسأله من مال نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who date the surah to Medina say it concerns an unnamed hypocrite; the occasion reports are attributed in part to Successors.
rows.anchor: والذين جعلوا السورة مدنية قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaduʿ means to shove someone away violently and coercively, as in the verse about being driven toward Hell.
rows.anchor: يوم يدعون إلى نار جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most muṣḥafs and commentaries title it Sūrat al-Kāfirūn, retaining the nominative wāw as in the Qurʾānic opening; some editions and works write genitive al-Kāfirīn, meaning a surah mentioning or addressing disbelievers.
rows.anchor: عنونت هذه السورة في المصاحف التي بأيدينا قديمها وحديثها وفي معظم التفاسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī titles it “Say: O disbelievers”; it and al-Ikhlāṣ are called the two purifiers because they clear associationism, and al-Ikhlāṣ is a shared title.
rows.anchor: عنونها البخاري في كتاب التفسير من صحيحه سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tawbah is also called al-Muqashqishah for cleansing hypocrisy, so this name is shared among three surahs and needs qualification.
rows.anchor: أن سورة براءة تسمى المقشقشة لأنها تقشقش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Additional titles are Sūrat al-ʿIbādah, reported by Saʿdī from Jamāl al-Qurrāʾ, and Sūrat al-Dīn in al-Fīrūzābādī’s Baṣāʾir.
rows.anchor: في بصائر ذوي التمييز للفيروز آبادي تسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan by consensus according to Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Ibn Kathīr; a Medinan view is reported from Ibn al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: في حكاية ابن عطية وابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is ranked eighteenth in revelation, after al-Māʿūn and before al-Fīl, and has six verses.
rows.anchor: بعد سورة الماعون وقبل سورة الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: According to reports by al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Isḥāq, four Quraysh elders interrupted the Prophet during circumambulation and proposed alternating worship for one year each to share the benefit.
rows.anchor: فيما حكاه الواحدي في أسباب النزول وابن إسحاق في السيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named leaders were al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; they argued each side might benefit if its worship proved superior.
rows.anchor: والوليد بن المغيرة ،  وأمية بن خلف ،  والعاص بن وائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet rejected associating anything with God, then recited the whole surah at the Sacred Mosque the next morning; the negotiators despaired.
rows.anchor: معاذ الله أن أشرك به غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh proposal aimed to exploit the Prophet’s eagerness for their conversion and tempt him to acknowledge the divinity of their idols.
rows.anchor: لأنهم رأوا حرصه على أن يؤمنوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the negotiators despaired and then harmed the Prophet and his companions.
rows.anchor: فيئسوا منه وآذوه وآذوا أصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s purpose is to end all hope that the Prophet will concede any part of their disbelief, in decisive terms covering present and future; Islam does not mix with shirk.
rows.anchor: وبهذا يعلم الغرض الذي اشتملت عليه وأنه تأييسهم من أن يوافقهم في شيء مما هم عليه من الكفر بالقول الفصل المؤكد في الحال والاستقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening with “Say” emphasizes that what follows is a message specifically to be conveyed, although the whole Qurʾān is commanded for delivery; Jumuʿah 62:6 is another such opening.
rows.anchor: للاهتمام بما بعد القول بأنه كلام يراد إبلاغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Five surahs begin with “Say”: al-Jinn, al-Kāfirūn, al-Ikhlāṣ, and the two refuge surahs; the first three convey a message, while the last two are protective utterances.
rows.anchor: فالثلاث الأول لقول يبلغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address targets the four negotiators in the occasion report; the vocative first secures their attention, and calling them disbelievers degrades them and declares disavowal without fear because God protects the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والنداء موجه إلى الأربعة الذين قالوا للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī quotes Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī: the Prophet was to address the leaders in their gathering as “O disbelievers,” a designation that would anger them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر بن الأنباري :  إن المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I do not worship what you worship” reports the Prophet’s own action.
rows.anchor: إخبار عن نفسه بما يحصل منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the imperfect verb and lā, the statement negates worship in future times; this follows al-Kashshāf and most Arabic grammarians.
rows.anchor: لا تحصل مني عبادتي ما تعبدون في أزمنة في المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalīl explains lan as originating in lā plus an, since adding an after lā reinforces future negation; this shows lā itself marks future negation.
rows.anchor: كانت مفيدة نفي الفعل في المستقبل

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Mālik, Abū Ḥayyān in his commentary on this surah, and al-Suhaylī in al-Rawḍ al-Unuf reject the majority analysis of lā’s future force.
rows.anchor: وخالفهم ابن مالك كما في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future denial that the Prophet worship their gods also implies he does not worship them now, since they proposed alternating only in a coming year.
rows.anchor: في الحال بدلالة فحوى الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominal “you are not worshippers” uses an active participle for the present, saying they will not change their current polytheism even now, as they proposed worshipping the Prophet’s Lord later.
rows.anchor: بمغيرين إشراككم الآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast between the two sentence forms is a feature of eloquent usage.
rows.anchor: وبهذَا تعلم وجه المخالفة بين نظم الجملتين في أسلوب الاستعمال البليغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This divinely informed prediction is a sign of prophethood: none of the four ever converted, and they died in shirk, as with the challenge in 2:24.
rows.anchor: من دلائل نبوءته نظير قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What I worship” refers to God; mā can denote rational as well as non-rational chosen beings, while man alone is restricted to rational reference, so no ambiguity results.
rows.anchor: فلا مانع من إطلاق ( ما ) على العاقل

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī says relative mā can intentionally create ambiguity and magnify grandeur, as in the Arabic praise of what thunder glorifies and in 91:5.
rows.anchor: وقال السهيلي في « الروض الأنف » :  إن ( ما ) الموصولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This clause coordinates with verse 3, appropriately following denial that they will worship God with the Prophet’s denial that he will worship their idols.
rows.anchor: عطف الجملة على الجملة لمناسبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw rules out treating this as a merely synonymous verbal emphasis of verse 2; instead the nominal sentence and active participle express a stable present state.
rows.anchor: اسم فاعل دالا على زمان الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After denying future worship in verse 2, the Prophet now explicitly denies present worship of idols, spelling out the implication to make their hopes completely futile.
rows.anchor: صرح هنا بما تقتضيه دلالة الفحوى على نفي أن يعبد آلهتهم في الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The additional wording thoroughly answers their proposal and rhetorically matches their rejected offer; it reinforces the meaning without making the sentence a syntactic synonym-based emphasis.
rows.anchor: فاقتضى الاعتماد على دلالة المنطوق إطنابا في الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāw cannot separate two clauses in verbal emphasis; grammarians favor thumma, and al-Raḍī additionally allows fāʾ for gradual escalation without chronological sequence.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز الفصل بين الجملتين بالواو لأن الواو لا يفصل بها بين الجملتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past tense in “what you worshipped” presents their idol worship as long-established and hints that the Prophet never worshipped idols; otherwise it would say “what we used to worship.”
rows.anchor: للدلالة على رسوخهم في عبادة الأصنام من أزمان مضت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause coordinates with verse 4, completes the contrast between the Prophet and them, and again reports that they will not worship God, strengthening the prophecy that all four died in disbelief.
rows.anchor: لبيان تمام الاختلاف بين حاله وحالهم وإخبار بأنهم لا يعبدون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the clause reinforces its meaning, but the wāw makes this coordination rather than syntactic emphasis, as in verse 4.
rows.anchor: وقد حصل من ذكر هذه الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the entire clause may be literal repetition, with its original coordinating wāw repeated and verse 4 parenthetically placed between repetition and what it reiterates.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون جملة { ولا أنتم عابدون ما أعبد } تأكيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repetition discredits their offer that they would worship the Lord of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من التأكيد تحقيق تكذيبهم في عرضهم أنهم يعبدون رب محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verse summarizes and seals the preceding emphases as a proverb, more concise and comprehensive than Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm’s verse about each side being content with its own position.
rows.anchor: تذييل وفذلكة للكلام السابق بما فيه من التأكيدات

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī says people should not quote the verse when parting, since the Qurʾān was revealed for reflection and obedience rather than quotation.
rows.anchor: في « تفسير الفخر » هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls al-Rāzī’s argument imprecise: quoting does not conflict with obeying, and quotation itself can express eloquence and readiness to act; this explanation was omitted from al-Rāzī’s draft.
rows.anchor: وهذا كلام غير محرر لأن التمثل به لا ينافي العمل بموجبه وما التمثل به إلا من تمام بلاغته واستعداد للعمل به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting each predicate restricts the other party’s religion to them and the speaker’s religion to him; this is individualizing restriction, and the lām conveys special attachment or entitlement.
rows.anchor: أي دينكم مقصور على الكون بأنه لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This restriction reflects the certainty that they will not embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: أي لأنهم محقق عدم إسلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn means creed and religious way: beliefs and knowledge that guide action; it is called dīn because its root sense involves dealing and recompense.
rows.anchor: وهو معلومات وعقائد يعتقدها المرء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers omit the first-person yāʾ after dīn, leaving kasrah for lightness; Yaʿqūb pronounces it in connected and paused reading, while its omission from the muṣḥaf spelling does not require omission in recitation.
rows.anchor: بدون ياء بعد النون على أن ياء المتكلم محذوفة للتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, al-Bazzī, Hishām, and Ḥafṣ read the yāʾ of “and to me” with fatḥah; Qunbul, Ibn Dhakwān, Abū Bakr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf read it quiescent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع والبزي عن ابن كثير وهشام عن ابن عامر وحفص عن عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse begins a new statement shifting from insult and rebuke to announcing Abū Lahab’s hopeless ruin: his property and earnings will save him from nothing in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: استئناف ابتدائي للانتقال من إنشاء الشتم والتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past “did not avail” makes his failure to be saved certain.
rows.anchor: والتعبير بالماضي في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā is negative, though it may also be read as an interrogative expressing rebuke and denial.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون استفهامية للتوبيخ والإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Māl means owned wealth, commonly camels among Arabs; ʿUmar’s saying and a line by Zuhayr attest that usage, while Medinans, Khaybar residents, and Bahrainis often use it for date palms.
rows.anchor: وغلب عند العرب إطلاقه على الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “what he earned” is a relative clause with an optionally omitted object pronoun, meaning what he amassed.
rows.anchor: موصول وصلته والعائد محذوف جوازا لأنه ضمير نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What he earned” can mean assets besides livestock—currency, weapons, estates, goods, and food.
rows.anchor: من نقود وسلاح وربع وعروض وطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “his wealth” includes everything, and “what he earned” specifies his own acquired wealth after inherited property: what he inherited from ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib versus what he himself acquired.
rows.anchor: وهو ما ورثه عن أبيه عبد المطلب وما كسبه هو بنفسه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports Abū Lahab claimed he would ransom himself with his wealth and children if his nephew’s message proved true; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن مسعود أن أبا لهب قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets “what he earned” as his children, since a child is his father’s earning.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : { ما كسب } هو ولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God specified these words for the Prophet’s refuge prayer, the command “Say” calls for preserving the exact wording and its hoped-for response; it creates an inward meaning rather than an instruction to perform an act.
rows.anchor: الأمر بالقول يقتضي المحافظة على هذه الألفاظ

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that when he asked the Prophet about the two refuge surahs, he replied that he had been told to say them and had conveyed them, so people should say them too.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since these words are Qurʾān, their wording is prescribed for refuge, and seeking protection uses both the meaning and the exact words, even the word “Say.”
rows.anchor: على ألفاظها متعينة والتعوذ يحصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command is addressed to the Prophet and, absent evidence of restriction, extends to the community; the Prophet taught companions the surah and used both refuge surahs for al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, as authenticated in Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: وإذ قد كان قرآنا كان خطاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم به يشمل الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command therefore addresses both the specified Prophet and anyone capable of being addressed, as contextual cues show; the first-person “I seek refuge” applies to every person commanded to recite.
rows.anchor: فتكون صيغة الأمر الموجهة إلى المخاطب مستعملة في معنيي الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿishah reports that during the Prophet’s final illness he breathed the refuge formulas over himself; as his illness worsened, she recited them and wiped with his hand for its blessing.
rows.anchor: وما روي عن عائشة قالت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting the formula over another is substitution for someone unable to perform self-protection because of incapacity, childhood, or not knowing the words.
rows.anchor: فذلك على نية النيابة عمن لا يحسن أن يعوذ نفسه بنفسه بتلك الكلمات لعجز أو صغر أو عدم حفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAwdh is seeking shelter in something that protects; ʿādha bi- means taking refuge in someone or a fort, istaʿādha asks another for protection, and ʿādha min means turning away from danger.
rows.anchor: اللجأ إلى شيء يقي من يلجأ إليه ما يخافه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-falaq means dawn; faʿl has a passive sense like al-ṣamad, since night is imagined as enclosed and splitting open to reveal morning.
rows.anchor: وهو فعل بمعنى مفعول مثل الصمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq literally means splitting something open from within and is metaphorically used for dawn emerging from night, as light’s appearance is also called bringing forth or stripping away darkness.
rows.anchor: واستعير لظهور الصبح بعد ظلمة الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Lord of dawn because He created the conditions for sunrise; this attribute is selected because night brings thieves, predators, venomous creatures, difficult travel, distant help, and intensified illness, and some misguided people treated night as an evil deity.
rows.anchor: لأنه الذي خلق أسباب ظهور الصبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning is to seek refuge in the dawn’s Creator from night’s evils: He can rescue a person at night as He rescued the world by creating morning, so this description prepares for the prayer’s answer.
rows.anchor: أعوذ بفالق الصبح منجاة من شرور الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The specific evils following the general “evil of what He created” comprise three kinds: a time when harm is common, people who make harming others their occupation, and people with a disposition that prompts injury.
rows.anchor: عطف أشياء خاصة هي مما شمله عموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “from the evil” after each conjunction is unnecessary grammatically but intensifies the plea and seeks a response through devotional elaboration.
rows.anchor: بعد حرف العطف في هذه الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāsiq describes night when darkness deepens; the root gh-s-q means to become dark, as in “until the night’s darkness” in 17:78.
rows.anchor: وصف الليل إذا اشتدت ظلمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The described noun is omitted because it is obvious from the modifier, as with “ships” in 42:32; the indefinite term means the genus of night and, in supplication, every night.
rows.anchor: صفة لموصوف محذوف لظهوره من معنى وصفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥarīrī’s “O people of this place, may you be spared harm” exemplifies an indefinite word used in a prayer to mean every harm.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الحريري في المقامة الخامسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive attachment of “evil” to “night” means evil occurring in that time, like “plotting by night and day” in 34:33.
rows.anchor: وإضافة الشر إلى غاسق من إضافة الاسم إلى زمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is singled out because thieves, predators, and vermin commonly cause harm then.
rows.anchor: تكثر فيه حوادث السوء من اللصوص والسباع والهوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “When it enters” restricts the prayer to intensified darkness, when criminals and predators exploit people’s sleep and heedlessness; the night is figuratively described as treacherous because betrayal increases then.
rows.anchor: أي إذا اشتدت ظلمته لأن ذلك وقت يتحينه الشطار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waqaba means to enter and penetrate; waqbah is a rock’s water-holding hollow, and the sun is said to set with the same verb.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { وقب } دخل وتغلغل في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer specifies the darkest time of night because it is the period when harm is most expected.
rows.anchor: وخص بالتعوذ أشد أوقات الليل توقعا لحصول المكروه
